name: Origami
tagline: A hosted chat interface for talking to large language models, with saved conversations instead of a dozen browser tabs.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Chat frontends over model APIs are the single most one-shottable category in software right now, because the hard part lives behind someone else's endpoint. An agent can produce a streaming chat UI with conversation history, model switching, system prompts and markdown rendering in a single session, and you pay raw token cost instead of a subscription margin. What you will not match on day one is the accumulated polish: keyboard flow, attachments, mobile behaviour, and the hundred small decisions that make a chat app feel calm. If the product's real pitch is something narrower than generic chat, a specific workflow, a curated agent, shared team context, discount that confidence accordingly. But the plain chat loop is a solved evening.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app that streams responses from your chosen model provider, stores every conversation in SQLite, and lets you switch models and system prompts mid-thread.
requirements: An API key from at least one model provider
Node 20 and a local machine or small VPS
Willingness to pay per token instead of per month
whatYouLose: Native mobile and a synced account across devices
Attachments, file parsing and image input unless you wire each one yourself
Shared conversations and anything resembling team workspaces
Provider fallbacks and rate limit handling when one API has a bad day
The maintained UI: your local build will feel like a prototype for a while
moatNotes: The moat in chat clients is taste and maintenance, not technology. Nobody has a defensible position on a text box.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a chat client is used dozens of times a day, and at that frequency friction is expensive. People pay to have someone else keep up with new models, handle attachments and long context, ship a working phone app, and make sure history is there when they open a different laptop. A self-hosted build covers the mechanics of the conversation but leaves you as the maintainer of your own daily driver, which is a job you did not want.
notes: The build takes an evening; keeping it pleasant for a year is the actual subscription you are cancelling.
prompt:
Build a local AI chat client in an empty folder. Stack, no substitutions:
Vite + React + TypeScript on the frontend, a small Express server in the same repo for API proxying, SQLite via better-sqlite3 for storage. No auth, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Requirements:
1. Single page app, two panes: conversation list on the left, active thread on the right.
2. Streaming responses. The Express server proxies to the model provider using server-sent events so the API key never reaches the browser.
3. Support two providers behind one interface: OpenAI-compatible chat completions and Anthropic messages. Read ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and OPENAI_API_KEY from .env, and ship a .env.example. Never hardcode keys.
4. A model picker in the composer. Model list lives in a single editable config file, not fetched, so I can paste in new model ids as they ship.
5. Per-conversation system prompt, editable at any time, applied to subsequent turns.
6. Persist conversations, messages, model used and token counts if the provider returns them. SQLite file at ./data/chat.db, created on first run.
7. Render assistant output as markdown with fenced code blocks, syntax highlighting and a copy button per block.
8. Keyboard first: Enter sends, Shift+Enter newlines, Cmd+K opens conversation search, Cmd+N starts a new thread.
9. Edit and resend any user message, which forks the thread rather than mutating history.
10. Export a conversation as markdown to the clipboard or a file.

Explicitly out of scope: file uploads, image input, tool calling, RAG, multi-user support, mobile layouts beyond basic responsiveness.

Deliver a README with setup in under five commands, seed the database on first run, and make npm run dev start both server and client together.
